questions.title: INNER JOIN vs. LEFT JOIN
questions.prompt: In SQL Server, what is the difference between an INNER JOIN and a LEFT JOIN? Specifically, what happens to rows that don't have a match on the other side in each case?
questions.modelAnswer: INNER JOIN returns only the rows where the ON condition evaluates true on both sides — any row from either table that has no match on the other side is dropped from the result entirely. LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the table named in the FROM clause (the 'left' table), whether or not it has a match in the table named after JOIN (the 'right' table). When a left-table row has no match, every column that would have come from the right table comes back as NULL instead of the row being dropped. 'Left' and 'right' describe position in the query text — the table in FROM is left, the table after JOIN is right — not anything about the size or importance of the data. A common real use of LEFT JOIN is combining it with WHERE <right-table-column> IS NULL to find rows that have no match at all, since that column can only be NULL if the join failed to find a partner row.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it with a concrete example: if I join Product to SalesOrderDetail with an INNER JOIN, I only see products that have actually sold — a product sitting in inventory with zero orders just disappears from the result, because there's nothing on the right side to pair it with. If my actual question is 'show me every product, including the ones that have never sold,' INNER JOIN can't answer that by definition, so I switch to a LEFT JOIN from Product. Now every product shows up, and for the ones with no matching order, the order columns just come back NULL. That NULL is actually useful — if I add WHERE OrderQty IS NULL to that LEFT JOIN, I've just built a 'products that have never sold' report, which is a query I get asked for constantly in a reporting role. The one thing I'm careful to remember is that left and right only refer to where I physically wrote the table in the query, not which table is 'bigger' or more important.
questions.example:
-- INNER JOIN: only products with at least one order line
SELECT p.Name, p.ListPrice, sod.OrderQty
FROM Production.Product AS p
INNER JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON p.ProductID = sod.ProductID;

-- LEFT JOIN: every product, NULL-filled when there's no match
SELECT p.Name, p.ListPrice, sod.OrderQty
FROM Production.Product AS p
LEFT JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON p.ProductID = sod.ProductID;

-- Finding products that have NEVER sold
SELECT p.Name
FROM Production.Product AS p
LEFT JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON p.ProductID = sod.ProductID
WHERE sod.ProductID IS NULL;
commonMistakes: Thinking 'left' and 'right' describe which table has more rows or matters more, instead of just position in the FROM/JOIN clause
Forgetting that unmatched right-side columns come back as NULL, then getting confused when COUNT() or SUM() on those columns behaves unexpectedly
Using INNER JOIN when the real goal is to find rows with no match — that specifically requires LEFT JOIN plus an IS NULL check
Not realizing WHERE runs after the join, so a WHERE clause on a right-side column can accidentally turn a LEFT JOIN back into something that behaves like an INNER JOIN
keyPoints: INNER JOIN returns only rows matching on both sides
LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the table named in FROM, matched or not
Left/right refer to position in the query, not data meaning or size
Unmatched right-side columns come back as NULL in a LEFT JOIN
LEFT JOIN + IS NULL is the standard pattern for finding unmatched rows

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what each join type returns
Explains NULL behavior for unmatched LEFT JOIN rows
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: WHERE vs. HAVING
questions.prompt: Why can't you filter on the result of an aggregate function (like AVG or COUNT) using a WHERE clause, and how does HAVING solve that problem? What is the correct logical order of FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, and ORDER BY?
questions.modelAnswer: WHERE is evaluated before GROUP BY runs, so at the point WHERE executes, groups and their aggregated values (like AVG(ListPrice)) don't exist yet — there's nothing for WHERE to compare against. HAVING is WHERE's counterpart for groups: it runs after GROUP BY has formed the groups and after the aggregate functions have been computed, so by the time HAVING evaluates, every group's aggregate already exists and can be filtered on. The correct logical processing order in T-SQL is: FROM (and JOIN) first, then WHERE filters individual rows, then GROUP BY forms groups, then HAVING filters those groups, then SELECT picks the columns/expressions to return, and finally ORDER BY sorts the final result. WHERE and HAVING aren't mutually exclusive — you commonly use WHERE to remove rows before grouping even starts, and HAVING to filter the groups that result.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of it as a timeline problem, not a syntax problem. If I write WHERE AVG(ListPrice) > 500, SQL Server throws an error, because logically WHERE runs before GROUP BY has even created any groups — there's no average to check yet. The moment I actually need to filter on an aggregated value, I move that condition to HAVING, which runs after the grouping and aggregation have already happened. In practice I use both together constantly: WHERE Color IS NOT NULL to throw out rows with no color recorded before I even start grouping, then GROUP BY Color, then HAVING AVG(ListPrice) > 500 to keep only the color groups whose average price clears that bar. I always come back to the same six-step order — FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY — whenever I'm unsure why a query is or isn't behaving the way I expect.
questions.example:
SELECT Color, AVG(ListPrice) AS AveragePrice
FROM Production.Product
WHERE Color IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY Color
HAVING AVG(ListPrice) > 500;
-- WHERE removes NULL-color rows before grouping; HAVING keeps only
-- the color groups whose computed average price exceeds 500.
commonMistakes: Writing WHERE AVG(ListPrice) > 500 and being surprised by the error instead of recognizing aggregates aren't available yet at that stage
Assuming WHERE and HAVING are interchangeable, rather than realizing WHERE filters rows and HAVING filters groups
Not knowing the logical processing order, which makes debugging any non-trivial query much harder
Putting a filter that doesn't need aggregation into HAVING instead of WHERE, which is valid but wastes work filtering rows that could have been removed earlier
keyPoints: WHERE filters individual rows and runs before GROUP BY
HAVING filters groups and runs after GROUP BY and aggregation
Logical order: FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> ORDER BY
WHERE and HAVING can and often should be used together

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why WHERE can't reference aggregates
Correctly states the logical processing order
Explains how WHERE and HAVING work together

questions.title: Write a GROUP BY aggregate query
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL query against AdventureWorks2012's Production.Product table that returns each distinct Color along with the count of products of that color and the average ListPrice for that color, excluding rows where Color is NULL.
questions.code:
-- Production.Product (AdventureWorks2012) has columns including:
-- ProductID, Name, Color, ListPrice
USE AdventureWorks2012;
GO
questions.modelAnswer: GROUP BY works in three conceptual steps: split the table into groups (one group per distinct Color value), aggregate within each group separately (COUNT and AVG each run once per group, not once overall), then combine the results into one row per group. Every column in SELECT must either be wrapped in an aggregate function or listed in GROUP BY — Color qualifies because it's the GROUP BY column; Name would not be allowed unaggregated here because it varies within a color group. Filtering out NULL colors belongs in WHERE, since that's a row-level filter that should happen before grouping, not a group-level filter.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write WHERE Color IS NOT NULL first, since that's just removing rows before grouping even starts — no reason to let NULL colors form their own group if the business doesn't care about them. Then GROUP BY Color splits the remaining rows into one bucket per color, and COUNT(*) plus AVG(ListPrice) each compute their own answer per bucket rather than one answer for the whole table. The result has exactly one row per distinct color — the same number of rows COUNT(DISTINCT Color) would report — which is a good sanity check I'd run after writing a query like this.
questions.example:
SELECT Color,
       COUNT(*) AS ProductCount,
       AVG(ListPrice) AS AveragePrice
FROM Production.Product
WHERE Color IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY Color
ORDER BY ProductCount DESC;
-- One row per distinct Color; COUNT and AVG are computed per color group.
commonMistakes: Adding Name or another non-aggregated, non-grouped column to SELECT and getting a GROUP BY error
Filtering NULL colors with HAVING instead of WHERE, doing unnecessary work by grouping rows that should have been excluded first
Forgetting WHERE Color IS NOT NULL entirely and getting an extra group for NULL
Confusing COUNT(*) (counts rows) with COUNT(Color) (counts non-NULL Color values) when NULLs are still present
keyPoints: GROUP BY splits rows into groups, aggregates within each, then combines into one row per group
Every SELECT column must be aggregated or included in GROUP BY
Row-level filters (like excluding NULL) belong in WHERE, before grouping
Result row count should match COUNT(DISTINCT <grouped column>)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct GROUP BY syntax and aggregate functions
Correctly excludes NULL colors with WHERE, not HAVING
Explains why the query is structured that way

questions.title: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and DENSE_RANK side by side
questions.prompt: Write a query that ranks products by ListPrice descending using ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), and DENSE_RANK() in the same result set, and explain how the three functions differ when two products are tied for the same price.
questions.modelAnswer: ROW_NUMBER() always produces unique, sequential numbers — even for genuinely tied values, it arbitrarily breaks the tie and gives one row a lower number than the other. RANK() gives tied rows the same number, but leaves a gap afterward: if two products tie for rank 1, the next distinct price gets rank 3, not 2, because RANK() accounts for how many rows were tied at the previous rank. DENSE_RANK() also gives tied rows the same number, but with no gap — the next distinct price after a tie at rank 1 gets rank 2. All three are computed with an OVER (ORDER BY ...) window clause and require no GROUP BY.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd run all three in one query so the difference is visible directly in the output rather than just described. If two products are tied for the most expensive, ROW_NUMBER() pretends there's no tie at all and numbers them 1 and 2 arbitrarily — which would misrepresent a genuine tie as a win. RANK() is honest about the tie: both get rank 1, but the next product jumps to rank 3, because two rows already occupied rank 1's 'slot.' DENSE_RANK() is also honest about the tie — both get rank 1 — but it only cares about distinct values, so the next price tier is rank 2 with no gap. Which one I pick depends on the business question: a sales leaderboard where two reps tied for second place genuinely skips third place calls for RANK(); a scale of distinct price tiers where I just want the next gap-free tier number calls for DENSE_RANK().
questions.example:
SELECT Name, ListPrice,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS RowNum,
       RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS Rank_,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS DenseRank_
FROM Production.Product
ORDER BY ListPrice DESC;
-- Tied prices: RowNum stays unique, Rank_ ties then skips ahead,
-- DenseRank_ ties with no gap.
commonMistakes: Assuming ROW_NUMBER() is 'safer' for ties when it actually hides them by assigning arbitrary unique numbers
Confusing RANK's gap-after-a-tie behavior with DENSE_RANK's no-gap behavior
Forgetting that ORDER BY inside OVER() determines which rows get which rank — changing it changes the whole result
Trying to use these functions without an OVER() clause, or expecting them to need a GROUP BY
keyPoints: ROW_NUMBER() always produces unique numbers, even for ties
RANK() ties share a number but the next value skips ahead by the tie size
DENSE_RANK() ties share a number with no gap for the next distinct value
All three run inside OVER (ORDER BY ...), no GROUP BY needed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct syntax for all three ranking functions
Accurately explains the tie-handling difference
Picks a sensible real-world scenario for each function

questions.title: Primary keys vs. foreign keys
questions.prompt: What does a PRIMARY KEY constraint guarantee about a column, and what does a FOREIGN KEY constraint enforce between two tables? What happens if you try to insert a row that violates a foreign key?
questions.modelAnswer: A primary key guarantees two things at once about a column (or set of columns): every value is unique, and no value is ever NULL — together that means a primary key value always identifies exactly one row. Creating a primary key without specifying otherwise also builds a clustered index on it by default, physically sorting the table by that key. A foreign key enforces referential integrity: every value in the foreign-key column must already exist as a primary-key value in the referenced table. Trying to insert or update a row with a foreign-key value that doesn't exist in the referenced table fails with error 547 — the database physically refuses to create the orphaned row. ON DELETE CASCADE changes the default behavior (which blocks deleting a referenced row while dependents still point to it) so that deleting a parent row automatically deletes its dependent rows too.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe the primary key as the table's identity guarantee — Production.Product's primary key, ProductID, means I can always find exactly one product for a given ID, never zero, never two. The foreign key is what makes a JOIN trustworthy: Product.ProductSubcategoryID is a foreign key to ProductSubcategory, so SQL Server physically won't let me insert a product pointing at a subcategory that doesn't exist. If I try, I get error 547, which is the database doing its job, not a bug to work around. I'm careful with ON DELETE CASCADE, though — it's convenient for cleaning up dependent rows automatically, but on a deep relationship chain it can silently delete far more data than I expect, so I think through the blast radius before turning it on.
commonMistakes: Thinking a primary key only guarantees uniqueness and forgetting it also guarantees NOT NULL
Not realizing a primary key builds a clustered index by default unless you explicitly say NONCLUSTERED
Assuming a foreign key violation is just a warning rather than a hard failure (error 547) that blocks the write
Adding ON DELETE CASCADE without considering how far the deletion could cascade through a longer relationship chain
keyPoints: Primary key = unique + NOT NULL, identifying exactly one row
Primary key creates a clustered index by default
Foreign key enforces that a value must exist as a primary key in another table
Violating a foreign key raises Error 547
ON DELETE CASCADE changes the default block-on-delete behavior

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes what a primary key guarantees
Correctly describes referential integrity and Error 547
Mentions the clustered index / cascade nuance

questions.title: Debugging a WHERE = NULL mistake
questions.prompt: A junior developer writes WHERE MiddleName = NULL to find customers with no middle name recorded, and gets zero rows back — even though many customers genuinely have a NULL MiddleName. What's actually wrong with that query, and how should they fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: NULL represents an unknown or not-applicable value, not zero or an empty string. Because it's unknown, NULL can't be said to equal anything — not even another NULL — so any comparison using the = operator against NULL evaluates to unknown (treated as false), never true. That means WHERE MiddleName = NULL will always return zero rows, regardless of how many rows actually have a NULL MiddleName, because the comparison can never succeed. The fix is to use the special IS NULL syntax instead: WHERE MiddleName IS NULL. IS NULL isn't a comparison operator — it's dedicated syntax built specifically to test for the absence of a value, and it works correctly where = cannot. The same logic applies to IS NOT NULL for the opposite case.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd point out is that this isn't a typo or syntax error — the query runs fine, it just silently returns the wrong answer, which is the dangerous kind of bug. I'd explain that NULL means 'unknown,' and you can't compare an unknown value to anything using = and expect a meaningful true or false — SQL Server treats that comparison as unknown, which gets filtered out just like false. So WHERE MiddleName = NULL isn't matching NULLs, it's failing to match anything at all. The fix is WHERE MiddleName IS NULL, which is purpose-built syntax for exactly this case rather than a regular comparison. If the goal were actually to display something readable instead of filtering, I'd reach for ISNULL(MiddleName, '(none)') or COALESCE for more than two fallback values.
commonMistakes: Not realizing the query runs without error and silently returns the wrong result, rather than throwing an obvious failure
Treating NULL as if it were an empty string or zero instead of 'unknown'
Using = NULL or <> NULL anywhere instead of IS NULL / IS NOT NULL
Confusing ISNULL() (replaces a NULL with a default, two arguments) with IS NULL (tests for NULL)
keyPoints: NULL means unknown/not applicable, not zero or empty string
= NULL always evaluates to unknown/false, never true
IS NULL / IS NOT NULL is the only correct way to test for NULL
ISNULL()/COALESCE() substitute a default value rather than test for NULL

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses why = NULL fails silently
Provides the correct fix (IS NULL)
Mentions ISNULL/COALESCE as a related but different tool

questions.title: CTEs vs. regular subqueries
questions.prompt: What is a Common Table Expression (CTE), and how does it differ from writing the same logic as a regular subquery? Why might you prefer a CTE?
questions.modelAnswer: A CTE (Common Table Expression) is a named, temporary result set defined at the top of a query with the WITH keyword. Functionally, it's equivalent to putting the same SELECT inside a subquery in the FROM clause — but instead of nesting it inline, you give it a name once and then reference that name like a real table in the statement that follows. This makes deeply nested subqueries much easier to read, especially when the same intermediate result needs to be referenced more than once in the outer query. A CTE is strictly temporary: it only exists for the single statement immediately following its WITH clause, is never saved anywhere, and disappears the moment that statement finishes — unlike a VIEW, which is a genuinely reusable, saved named query.
questions.professionalAnswer: I reach for a CTE mainly for readability. A subquery nested three levels deep inside a FROM clause gets hard to read fast — you end up mentally tracking which closing parenthesis belongs to which level. If I give that same logic a name with WITH CategoryAverages AS (...), I can read the outer query almost like English: 'from CategoryAverages, where...' That's especially valuable when I need to reference the same intermediate calculation more than once in the final query, since a CTE lets me do that without repeating the underlying SELECT. The one thing I always clarify for someone newer to this is that a CTE isn't a saved object — it only lives for the one statement right after it, so if I need that same logic reused across multiple separate queries, a VIEW is the right tool, not a CTE.
questions.example:
WITH CategoryAverages AS (
    SELECT ProductSubcategoryID, AVG(ListPrice) AS AvgPrice
    FROM Production.Product
    GROUP BY ProductSubcategoryID
)
SELECT ca1.ProductSubcategoryID, ca1.AvgPrice
FROM CategoryAverages AS ca1
WHERE ca1.AvgPrice > (SELECT AVG(AvgPrice) FROM CategoryAverages);
-- CategoryAverages is referenced twice in one statement -- hard to
-- do cleanly with a nested subquery instead.
commonMistakes: Thinking a CTE is saved/reusable across separate queries like a VIEW, rather than scoped to one statement
Not taking advantage of referencing the same CTE multiple times in the outer query
Assuming a CTE is always faster than a subquery -- it's primarily a readability tool, not automatically a performance one
Forgetting the WITH keyword needs to be the first word of the batch (or preceded by a semicolon) in some contexts
keyPoints: CTE = a named, temporary result set defined with WITH
Functionally equivalent to a FROM-clause subquery, but far more readable
Can be referenced multiple times in the statement that follows it
Scoped to one statement only -- not saved like a VIEW

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines what a CTE is
Explains the readability/multiple-reference advantage
Correctly notes the CTE is scoped to one statement, unlike a VIEW

questions.title: Write a parameterized stored procedure
questions.prompt: Write a stored procedure named usp_GetProductsAbovePrice that accepts a @MinPrice parameter defaulting to 100, and returns the Name and ListPrice of every product in Production.Product with a ListPrice at or above that value, ordered by price descending. Then show how you'd call it both with and without supplying a value for @MinPrice.
questions.modelAnswer: A parameter is declared right after the procedure name, before the AS keyword, and behaves like a normal variable throughout the procedure body — it's just pre-populated from whatever the caller passes in. Giving a parameter a default value (@MinPrice MONEY = 100) makes it optional: if the caller doesn't supply a value, SQL Server uses the default automatically. Calling the procedure with named notation (EXEC usp_GetProductsAbovePrice @MinPrice = 500) is unambiguous and order-independent, which is why it's preferred over positional calling once a procedure has more than one parameter.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write the parameter with a sensible default so the procedure is usable both ways out of the box. The body itself is just the same filtered, sorted SELECT I'd write ad hoc, except @MinPrice stands in for whatever literal value I'd otherwise hard-code. Calling it with EXEC usp_GetProductsAbovePrice; uses the default of 100 automatically, and calling it with @MinPrice = 500 overrides that for just this call. I always call with named parameters -- @MinPrice = 500 instead of just 500 -- because the moment a procedure picks up a second or third parameter, positional calling becomes an easy way to silently pass values to the wrong parameter.
questions.example:
CREATE PROCEDURE usp_GetProductsAbovePrice
    @MinPrice MONEY = 100
AS
BEGIN
    SELECT Name, ListPrice
    FROM Production.Product
    WHERE ListPrice >= @MinPrice
    ORDER BY ListPrice DESC;
END;
GO

EXEC usp_GetProductsAbovePrice @MinPrice = 500; -- overrides the default
EXEC usp_GetProductsAbovePrice;                 -- uses the default, 100
commonMistakes: Forgetting the default value, which forces every caller to always supply @MinPrice even when a sensible default exists
Calling the procedure positionally once it has multiple parameters, risking values landing in the wrong parameter
Putting the parameter declaration after AS instead of before it
Hard-coding the price threshold inside the procedure body instead of parameterizing it, defeating the point of a reusable procedure
keyPoints: Parameters are declared before AS and behave like pre-populated variables
A default value makes a parameter optional
Named notation (@Param = value) is unambiguous and order-independent
EXEC without a value for an optional parameter falls back to its default

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct CREATE PROCEDURE syntax with a default parameter
Correct query logic (filter + sort)
Shows both calling styles (with and without override)

questions.title: Diagnosing an accidental Cartesian product
questions.prompt: A query joining a 500-row Products table to a 100,000-row OrderDetail table unexpectedly returns 50 million rows instead of something in the few-hundred-thousand range. What almost certainly went wrong, and how would you confirm it?
questions.modelAnswer: 50 million is exactly 500 times 100,000 -- the row-count signature of a Cartesian product, where every row of one table gets paired with every row of the other instead of only matching rows being paired. The most common real-world cause isn't a deliberate CROSS JOIN -- it's a missing or ineffective ON condition on what was meant to be a normal join: either the ON clause is left out entirely (old-style comma join with no join condition), or it exists but evaluates to true for nearly every row combination (for example ON p.Name IS NOT NULL, which doesn't actually relate the two tables). To confirm it, check the join's ON clause first for a missing or non-relating condition, and as a general habit, sanity-check the row count after any join: if two tables of roughly 500 and 100,000 rows produce millions of result rows instead of a number in that rough range, that's an immediate signal to re-check the ON clause rather than assume the data is simply that large.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd notice is that 50 million is suspiciously close to 500 times 100,000 -- that's the fingerprint of a Cartesian product, not a coincidence. My first move is to go straight to the ON clause of the join and check two things: is it missing entirely, which happens with old comma-style joins that have no join condition at all, or does it exist but not actually relate the two tables -- something like ON p.Name IS NOT NULL, which is true for almost every row and produces a Cartesian product in disguise even though there's technically an ON clause sitting there. Once I fix the condition to something that actually ties the tables together, like p.ProductID = sod.ProductID, I'd re-run the query and expect the row count to land in the same rough range as the bigger of the two tables, not multiply them together. I've made this a habit on every join I write now: sanity-check the row count before trusting the result.
questions.example:
-- BUG: no join condition at all -- a Cartesian product
SELECT p.Name, sod.OrderQty
FROM Production.Product AS p, Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod;

-- BUG: ON clause exists but doesn't relate the tables
SELECT p.Name, sod.OrderQty
FROM Production.Product AS p
INNER JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON p.Name IS NOT NULL;

-- FIXED: a real join condition tying the tables together
SELECT p.Name, sod.OrderQty
FROM Production.Product AS p
INNER JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON p.ProductID = sod.ProductID;
commonMistakes: Assuming the data itself is just 'that big' instead of suspecting the join condition first
Not recognizing that an ON clause can exist and still produce a Cartesian product if it doesn't genuinely relate the tables
Never sanity-checking row counts after writing a join, so the problem isn't caught until it hits production
Confusing this with a deliberate CROSS JOIN -- the accidental version almost always comes from a broken or missing ON condition on what was meant to be a normal join
keyPoints: Row count multiplying (500 x 100,000) instead of adding is the signature of a Cartesian product
Most accidental Cartesian products come from a missing or non-relating ON clause
Old-style comma joins with no ON clause default to a Cartesian product
An ON clause that's technically present but true for nearly every row is just as dangerous as none at all
Sanity-check row counts after any join as a standing habit

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the Cartesian product and the row-count math
Correctly identifies missing/ineffective ON clause as the cause
Describes a practical way to catch this before production

questions.title: SSIS: Control Flow vs. Data Flow
questions.prompt: In SSIS, what's the difference between the Control Flow and a Data Flow, and why does a Data Flow Task live inside the Control Flow rather than being its own kind of package?
questions.modelAnswer: Every SSIS package runs on two separate engines. The runtime engine manages the Control Flow -- task order, precedence constraints, logging, event handlers, and variables -- and is active any time a package validates or runs, in development or production. The data flow engine is a specialized engine that a Data Flow Task hands off to, dedicated purely to moving and transforming rows. The Data Flow tab is a completely separate design surface from Control Flow, with its own Toolbox of sources, transformations, and destinations -- none of the Control Flow tasks (Execute SQL, For Loop, Sequence Container) belong there. A Data Flow Task is just a task sitting on the Control Flow, like any other: a package can contain more than one Data Flow Task, each with its own completely independent data flow, and the Control Flow is what sequences them (with precedence constraints) and decides when each one runs.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe it as two engines working together rather than one. Control Flow is the orchestration layer -- it decides the order things happen in, handles looping, branching, and error handling at the task level. The moment I drop a Data Flow Task onto the Control Flow and double-click into it, I'm on a completely different surface with a different Toolbox -- sources, transformations, destinations -- because that's where rows actually move and get transformed, powered by a separate data flow engine built for exactly that job. A real package I'd build often has multiple Data Flow Tasks sequenced on the Control Flow with precedence constraints -- say, one to stage raw extracts, a second to clean and conform them, a third to load the warehouse -- and each one is its own self-contained pipeline I can open, debug, and reason about independently of the others.
commonMistakes: Thinking Control Flow and Data Flow are the same design surface instead of two separate tabs with different Toolboxes
Assuming a package can only have one Data Flow Task
Believing Data Flow Task components (sources, transformations, destinations) can be dropped directly onto the Control Flow surface
Not realizing each Data Flow Task's data flow is completely independent -- nothing is shared between two Data Flow Tasks in the same package
keyPoints: Runtime engine manages Control Flow: task order, logging, event handlers, variables
Data flow engine moves and transforms rows inside a Data Flow Task
Data Flow tab has its own Toolbox, separate from Control Flow
A package can hold multiple independent Data Flow Tasks, sequenced on the Control Flow

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes the two engines
Explains why a Data Flow Task sits on the Control Flow
Mentions multiple independent data flows in one package

questions.title: Building a simple SSIS data flow
questions.prompt: Describe, step by step, how you'd configure a Data Flow in SSIS that extracts FirstName and LastName from AdventureWorks2012's Person.Person table using an OLE DB Source, builds a FullName column by concatenating them with a Derived Column transformation, and loads the result into a staging table using an OLE DB Destination in fast-load mode.
questions.modelAnswer: First, add an OLE DB Source to the Data Flow, double-click it, pick the OLE DB connection manager pointed at AdventureWorks2012, set the data access mode to 'Table or view' (or 'SQL command' for a filtered query), and select Person.Person. On the Columns page, select FirstName and LastName as the external columns to bring into the data flow, and use Preview to confirm the rows look right before finishing. Next, drag a Derived Column transformation onto the surface and connect the source's output to it. Add a new derived column named FullName, set it to '<add as new column>' (not Replace, since FirstName and LastName should remain untouched), and set the expression to FirstName + " " + LastName -- the editor will auto-detect the resulting data type. Finally, add an OLE DB Destination downstream, connect the Derived Column's output to it, point it at the staging table, and set its data access mode to 'Table or view - fast load' so the load uses SQL Server's bulk-insert mechanism instead of row-by-row inserts. On the Mappings page, map FirstName, LastName, and FullName to the matching destination columns, making sure every non-nullable destination column has a mapping, since an unmapped NOT NULL column fails the load at run time.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through it in the same order the data actually flows. Source first: OLE DB Source pointed at Person.Person, data access mode set to Table or view, and I always hit Preview before moving on so I'm not debugging a typo three components downstream. Then the Derived Column transformation -- I add FullName as a brand-new column rather than replacing anything, with the expression FirstName + " " + LastName, and I let the editor auto-infer the data type rather than fighting it. Last is the OLE DB Destination, and the one detail I wouldn't skip is switching its data access mode to Table or view - fast load, because that uses SQL Server's bulk-insert mechanism instead of inserting row by row -- it's a meaningful speed difference on anything beyond a trivial row count. On the Mappings page I'd specifically double-check that every NOT NULL column on the staging table has something mapped to it, because an unmapped nullable column is harmless but an unmapped non-nullable one fails the whole load at run time.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to use Preview on the OLE DB Source before moving downstream, catching a bad configuration late
Setting the Derived Column to Replace when the intent was to add FullName as a new column alongside the originals
Leaving the OLE DB Destination on plain 'Table or view' mode instead of 'fast load,' losing the bulk-insert performance benefit
Leaving a non-nullable destination column unmapped on the Mappings page, which fails the load at run time
keyPoints: OLE DB Source: pick connection, data access mode, and preview before finishing
Derived Column: choose add-new vs. replace deliberately

questions.title: One bad row shouldn't fail the whole load
questions.prompt: An SSIS package fails completely the moment a single row fails to convert during a Data Flow. How would you change the package so the other 9,999,999 good rows still load, with the bad row captured separately for review?
questions.modelAnswer: By default, most data flow components treat any row-level problem as fatal -- 'Fail Component' is the default disposition on both errors (an unrecoverable conversion failure, producing a NULL) and truncations (data cut short but still usable). The fix is to open the failing component's Configure Error Output dialog and change the Error (and/or Truncation) disposition from Fail Component to Redirect Row for the relevant column(s). That exposes a second, red error-output path out of the component. Connect that error output to a separate destination -- commonly a Flat File Destination writing to something like rejected_rows.txt -- so bad rows land there instead of stopping the task. SSIS automatically adds two columns to a redirected row, ErrorCode and ErrorColumn, identifying what went wrong and where; a Script Component calling GetErrorDescription() against ErrorCode can turn that into a readable message before it's written out. The main path continues on to the real destination untouched, so the 9,999,999 good rows still load.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd point out first that the default behavior -- Fail Component on both Error and Truncation -- is exactly why one bad row takes down the whole load, and that's rarely what anyone actually wants in production. My fix is to open Configure Error Output on the component that's failing, select the column (or columns) causing the problem, and change the Error disposition to Redirect Row. That gives the component a second, red output path I can wire into its own destination -- usually a flat file for rejected rows -- so the bad row gets written somewhere reviewable instead of killing the task. SSIS tacks on ErrorCode and ErrorColumn automatically for every redirected row, and if I want that to actually be readable instead of just a number, I'd route it through a Script Component that calls GetErrorDescription() first. The main path keeps running untouched, so the good 9,999,999 rows load exactly as before -- the only thing that changes is where the bad row ends up.
commonMistakes: Not realizing 'Fail Component' is the default on every column's Error and Truncation settings until changed
Confusing an Error (unrecoverable, produces NULL) with a Truncation (data cut short but usable) -- they're configured independently
Forgetting to actually connect the red error-output path to a destination after enabling Redirect Row
Leaving ErrorCode/ErrorColumn as raw numbers in the output file instead of resolving them with GetErrorDescription() for someone reviewing the rejects
keyPoints: Default disposition on error/truncation is Fail Component -- that's why one bad row kills the task
Redirect Row sends the failing row down a second, red error-output path instead
ErrorCode and ErrorColumn are added automatically to a redirected row
The main (green) path continues loading good rows untouched

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the default Fail Component behavior as the cause
Correctly proposes Redirect Row via Configure Error Output

questions.title: The SSISDB catalog
questions.prompt: What is the SSISDB catalog, and why does deploying an SSIS project to it require CLR integration to be enabled on the SQL Server instance?
questions.modelAnswer: The SSISDB catalog is the modern, production home for deployed SSIS projects -- it is not a separate service, but a real database named SSISDB hosted inside an actual instance of the SQL Server Database Engine. SQL Server doesn't create it automatically; it's provisioned once per instance by right-clicking Integration Services Catalogs in Object Explorer and selecting Create Catalog. Once created, the catalog becomes the single place where a deployed project's packages, parameters, environments, permissions, and full execution history live, all queryable with T-SQL. CLR integration has to be enabled because the catalog's functionality -- versioning, parameterization, execution tracking -- is implemented using CLR stored procedures (.NET code running inside SQL Server), so the instance-level CLR integration feature must be turned on for the catalog to work at all. Creating the catalog also requires a master key password, which protects the database master key SSISDB uses to encrypt sensitive parameter and connection manager values.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame this around the design-time versus run-time split: everything built in SSDT lives on a developer's own machine with no server involved until a deliberate deploy. SSISDB is that run-time destination -- a real database, not a special service, that every deployed project needs to exist before you can deploy anything to it at all. The reason CLR integration has to be turned on first is that the catalog's own stored procedures are written in .NET, not plain T-SQL, so without CLR integration enabled at the instance level, those procedures simply can't run. When I create the catalog I'm also asked for a master key password, which I'd treat as something to store securely, since it (or a backup of the master key) is what lets you recover the catalog onto a different instance later if you ever need to.
commonMistakes: Thinking SSISDB is a separate Windows service rather than a database inside the SQL Server Database Engine
Assuming the catalog is created automatically when Integration Services is installed
Not knowing CLR integration is a prerequisite because the catalog's stored procedures are CLR-based
Losing or forgetting the master key password, which is needed to recover the catalog onto a different instance

It's created once per instance via Create Catalog in Object Explorer
CLR integration is required because the catalog's stored procedures are implemented in .NET
The master key password protects encrypted sensitive catalog data and is needed for recovery
