questions.title: SSRS: data source vs. dataset
questions.prompt: In SSRS Report Builder, what's the difference between a data source and a dataset, and why does the distinction between 'embedded' and 'shared' matter once you have five reports that all need the same connection?
questions.modelAnswer: A data source is the connection information -- server, database, and credential method -- while a dataset is a query run against that connection, producing the actual rows and columns a report uses. They're always a pair: a data source without a dataset is a connection to nowhere in particular, and a dataset needs a data source to run against. Both come in two flavors: embedded, saved inside one report only, and shared, published once to the Report Server and referenced by any report that needs it. With five reports all pointing at the same database, an embedded data source means maintaining five separate copies of the same connection string -- if the server name changes, all five need updating individually. A shared data source centralizes that: change the server name in one place, and every report referencing that shared data source picks up the change automatically.
questions.professionalAnswer: New report authors often use 'data source' to mean the whole thing, but I'd keep the two separate: the data source is just the plumbing -- server, database, how to authenticate -- and the dataset is the actual query that runs through that plumbing to get rows. Once I have more than one or two reports hitting the same database, I move the data source to shared rather than embedded, because the alternative is five copies of the same connection string scattered across five report files. If that server ever gets renamed or moved, a shared data source means I fix it in exactly one place and every report referencing it just picks up the change; with embedded data sources I'd be opening and editing five separate reports by hand.
commonMistakes: Conflating 'data source' and 'dataset' as the same object
Defaulting every data source to embedded even when multiple reports share the same connection
Not realizing a shared data source change propagates automatically to every report referencing it
Forgetting a dataset still needs a data source behind it -- neither is useful alone
keyPoints: Data source = connection info; dataset = the query run against it
Embedded = lives in one report only; shared = published once, reused by many
Shared data sources centralize connection-string maintenance
A data source and dataset are always a pair

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes data source from dataset
Correctly explains embedded vs. shared
Gives a concrete maintenance-cost reason for using shared

questions.title: Building cascading parameters
questions.prompt: Walk through how you'd build a three-level cascading parameter set in SSRS -- Country, then State, then City -- so that picking a Country narrows the State list, and picking a State narrows the City list. What has to exist at each level, and why does the order of the parameters matter?
questions.modelAnswer: A cascading parameter setup isn't one property to flip on -- it's a chain of separate datasets, each one filtered by the parameter chosen before it. For the State dataset, I'd add a filter on its Filters tab where Expression is the state's country column, Operator is '=', and Value is [@CountryParameter] -- the shorthand referencing the Country parameter's current value. The City dataset gets its own filter the same way, built against [@StateParameter]. Each level needs its own dataset and its own filter referencing the parameter one level up; there's no single dialog that shows the whole chain at once. Order matters because the parameters' position under the Parameters node in the Report Data pane is the order the reader is prompted for them at run time, and because a dataset's filter can't reference a parameter value that hasn't been chosen yet -- Country must be listed before State, and State before City, or the chain breaks.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build this as three datasets, not one clever setting. The Country dataset is unfiltered -- it just lists every country. The State dataset gets a filter on its Filters tab: Expression is the state's country column, Operator is =, Value is [@CountryParameter]. The City dataset mirrors that pattern one level down, filtered on [@StateParameter]. The part that trips people up is parameter order in the Report Data pane -- it's not cosmetic, it's literally the order the reader gets prompted, and a parameter can't reference a value that doesn't exist yet, so Country has to come before State, and State before City, or the whole chain is broken from the start. Once it's wired up correctly, the reader experience is exactly what you'd expect: picking a country narrows the state dropdown, picking a state narrows the city dropdown, each step one level down the same chain.
commonMistakes: Looking for one dialog that configures the whole cascade at once, instead of building a filter on each dataset individually
Forgetting a dataset's Filters tab is where the actual cascading mechanism lives
Getting the parameter order wrong in the Report Data pane, breaking the dependency chain
Not realizing the cascading mechanism is identical for single-value and multi-value parameters (just = vs. In as the operator)
keyPoints: Cascading parameters require a chain of separate, filtered datasets -- not a single setting
Each dataset's Filters tab references the parameter one level up ([@ParameterName])
Parameter order in the Report Data pane determines both prompt order and dependency validity
A parameter can't be referenced by a filter before it's been chosen

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the chain of filtered datasets
Correctly describes the Filters tab mechanism (Expression/Operator/Value)
Explains why parameter order matters

questions.title: A subscription that stopped delivering
questions.prompt: A user says their SSRS report subscription, scheduled to e-mail them every morning at 6 AM, hasn't delivered anything in three days. What are the most likely causes, and where would you look first?
questions.modelAnswer: The first place to check is the subscription's own Result column on the report's Subscriptions management page -- it holds the outcome or error message from the most recent run, and is the fastest way to see whether the subscription is even firing or failing silently. Beyond that, the underlying mechanism is: a schedule writes to the report server database and creates a SQL Server Agent job; when that job fires, it drops an event into a queue the Scheduling and Delivery Processor polls (by default every 10 seconds), which then runs the report and hands the result to the delivery extension. Likely causes include: the schedule (shared or report-specific) being paused or deleted, SQL Server Agent being stopped during that window (scheduled operations that should have fired are simply lost, not queued to catch up later), the report's data source credentials having expired or changed (subscriptions run unattended and need stored or no credentials), or a parameter that used to have a default value no longer having one. Using Run Now on the Subscriptions page is a good way to test immediately rather than waiting for the next scheduled time.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start at the Subscriptions page for that report and check the Result column first -- that tells me in one glance whether the subscription is firing and failing, or not firing at all. If it's failing with a credential error, the most common cause is the data source's stored credentials expiring, since a subscription runs unattended and can't prompt anyone to log in. If there's no result at all for three days, I'd check whether SQL Server Agent was stopped during that window, since a schedule is backed by a real Agent job, and if the server was down when it should have fired, Reporting Services doesn't queue it to catch up -- it's just gone. I'd also check whether the schedule itself -- shared or report-specific -- got paused or deleted; if a shared schedule was deleted, Reporting Services actually clones it into individual report-specific schedules automatically, so that's less likely to be a silent failure, but worth confirming. Once I have a theory, Run Now on the subscription is the fastest way to test it without waiting for 6 AM to come around again.
commonMistakes: Not checking the subscription's Result column first, which is the fastest diagnostic signal available
Assuming a missed subscription will 'catch up' automatically -- a window where SQL Server Agent was down is simply lost
Forgetting subscriptions require stored (or no) credentials and default parameter values, since they run unattended
Not knowing a shared schedule being paused silently stops every subscription referencing it
keyPoints: Check the Result column on the Subscriptions page first
A schedule is backed by a real SQL Server Agent job -- if Agent was down, that run is lost, not queued
Subscriptions need stored/no credentials and default parameter values since they run unattended
Run Now is the fastest way to test a fix without waiting for the next scheduled time

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies where to check first (Result column)
Lists plausible real causes (credentials, Agent downtime, paused schedule)
Describes a practical verification step (Run Now)

questions.title: Report server architecture
questions.prompt: Describe the pieces of a native-mode SQL Server Reporting Services installation. What does the Report Server service actually do, and why are there two separate databases behind it instead of one?
questions.modelAnswer: A native-mode report server centers on the Report Server service, a Windows service that hosts the Report Server web service, runs background processing (scheduled operations, report delivery), and turns a report definition into a rendered report. The Report Server web service is the actual communications interface -- every client, including the web portal, Report Builder, SSDT, and rs.exe, talks to the report server through this web service, never around it. The web portal is the browser-based front end built on top of that web service (available only in native mode, not SharePoint-integrated mode), where users browse folders, run reports, subscribe, and manage permissions. Two databases are created together: ReportServer stores everything that must survive a restart -- reports, shared data sources, folders, subscriptions, schedules, snapshots, security settings, and encrypted credentials -- while ReportServerTempDB stores session/execution data, cached reports, and working tables that don't need to persist, and (unlike ReportServer) won't be automatically re-created if missing.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd lay out four pieces. The Report Server service is the Windows service at the center of everything -- it's always running, hosting the web service and doing the actual work of rendering reports. The Report Server web service is the real communications layer: whether it's the web portal, Report Builder, or a script using rs.exe, every one of them talks through this web service, not directly to the databases. The web portal is the part end users actually see -- the browsable, human-facing UI built on top of that web service. And then there are the two databases, which get created together and serve very different purposes: ReportServer is the one that has to survive a restart -- it's where reports, schedules, subscriptions, and security settings actually live -- while ReportServerTempDB is disposable working space for session data and cached output that Reporting Services periodically cleans out on its own, and critically, it won't come back automatically if it's deleted the way ReportServer would.
commonMistakes: Thinking the web portal and the web service are the same thing, or interchangeable URLs (/reports vs. /reportserver are different)
Assuming there's only one database behind a report server
Not knowing ReportServerTempDB won't auto-recreate itself if it's missing, unlike ReportServer
Thinking users or tools query the ReportServer/ReportServerTempDB databases directly instead of always going through the report server service
keyPoints: Report Server service hosts the web service and does background processing/rendering
Report Server web service is the real client-facing communications interface
Web portal is the browser UI, built on top of the web service, native-mode only
ReportServer persists content; ReportServerTempDB holds disposable session/cache data

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the Report Server service and web service roles
Correctly explains why two databases exist and what each stores
Mentions the web portal as a distinct, native-mode-only piece

questions.title: Measures vs. calculated columns in Power BI
questions.prompt: What's the difference between a calculated column and a measure in Power BI, and what's a simple rule for deciding which one you need for a given situation?
questions.modelAnswer: A calculated column is computed once, when data is entered or refreshed, and stored per row in row context -- it adds to the model's size and updates only when the table refreshes. A measure is computed dynamically every time it's viewed, evaluated in filter context (whatever's currently filtering the report), and isn't stored at all -- it recalculates instantly as filters change. The decision rule is: do you need to slice, filter, or group by this value, or just display a summarized number? If you need a new category to filter, group, or put in a slicer/legend/axis, you need a calculated column, because only columns are filterable. If you need a calculated number that summarizes -- a total, average, ratio, or projection -- you need a measure. Choosing wrong doesn't throw an error: a calculated column used where a measure was needed freezes at refresh-time values and goes silently stale as filters change; a measure used where a column was needed simply can't be dragged into a slicer or axis at all.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd give the one-question test I actually use: am I going to filter or group by this, or am I just going to display a summarized number? A customer loyalty tier based on total purchases is something I'd want in a slicer, so that's a calculated column. Total revenue that should recalculate as someone clicks through a report is a measure. The part I'd specifically warn a newer analyst about is that getting this wrong doesn't throw an error -- it just quietly produces the wrong behavior. A calculated column written where a measure belonged freezes at whatever it computed during the last refresh and goes stale the moment someone applies a filter; a measure written where a column belonged simply won't let you drag it into a slicer at all, since measures aren't filterable, only summarizable.
questions.example:
CityState = [City] & "," & [State]                              -- calculated column: used to group/display
Projected Sales = SUM('Reseller Sales'[Last Years Sales]) * 1.06  -- measure: dynamic, filter-context aware
commonMistakes: Writing a calculated column when a dynamically-recalculating measure was actually needed
Trying to drag a measure into a slicer or axis and not understanding why it isn't allowed
Not realizing calculated columns add to model size on every row, while measures add none
Assuming a wrong choice will throw an obvious error instead of silently producing stale or unusable results
keyPoints: Calculated column: computed once per row, stored, row context, filterable
Measure: computed dynamically, not stored, filter context, summarizable only
Decision rule: filter/group by it -> column; summarize/display it -> measure
Getting it wrong doesn't error -- it silently misbehaves

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes storage/evaluation differences
States a clear, usable decision rule
Explains the silent-failure consequence of choosing wrong

questions.title: Import vs. DirectQuery
questions.prompt: What's the core trade-off between Import and DirectQuery storage modes in Power BI, and why can you convert a DirectQuery table to Import but never the other way around?
questions.modelAnswer: Import copies the data into the Power BI file: visuals read from memory, so they're fast, and the model has full DAX feature support, but the data is only as fresh as the last refresh and is limited by file size (roughly a 1 GB typical cap). DirectQuery leaves the data in the source and queries it live every time a visual loads: it handles very large sources and gives truly real-time data, but visual speed depends entirely on the source's own speed, and some DAX/modeling features are restricted. Import is the default choice for most real reports and for learning, because of full feature support and no dependency on a live connection while working; DirectQuery earns its place when the source is too large to import practically, the data must be truly real-time, or a security policy requires data to never leave its source system. You can convert a DirectQuery table to Import because that's simply choosing to copy and cache data that was already being queried live -- but going the other direction would mean somehow 'un-caching' data and re-establishing a live query path, which isn't a simple reversal, so Power BI doesn't support converting Import back to DirectQuery.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame it as a speed-versus-freshness-versus-scale trade-off. Import is fast because everything's sitting in memory, and it gets full DAX support with no dependency on the source being reachable while I work -- that's why it's the default for basically every lesson and most real reports. DirectQuery trades that speed for currency and scale: the data never leaves the source, so it's always live, and there's no 1 GB-ish file-size ceiling, but now every visual's performance is only as good as the source database's performance, and some features aren't available. The one-way-door detail I'd flag explicitly: you can always switch a DirectQuery table to Import, since that's just deciding to start caching data you were already querying live, but you can't go back -- there's no clean way to 'un-cache' Import data and reconnect it as a live query, so if I'm unsure which mode I'll end up needing, I start with DirectQuery and convert later rather than the reverse.
commonMistakes: Assuming DirectQuery is always 'better' because it's real-time, ignoring the source-dependent performance cost
Not knowing Import has a practical file-size ceiling (around 1 GB)
Forgetting some DAX/modeling features are restricted under DirectQuery
Not realizing the Import conversion is one-directional -- DirectQuery to Import only, never back
keyPoints: Import: data copied into the file, fast, full feature support, refresh-dependent freshness
DirectQuery: data stays in source, live, scales to large sources, source-dependent speed
Import is the default for most reports; DirectQuery fits huge/real-time/security-constrained sources
You can convert DirectQuery to Import, never the reverse

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the Import vs. DirectQuery trade-off
Correctly explains the one-directional conversion
Gives a sensible real scenario for choosing DirectQuery

questions.title: Write a CALCULATE-based DAX measure
questions.prompt: Write a DAX measure called 'Blue Revenue' that sums SalesAmount from a Sales table, but only for rows where the related Product table's Color column equals 'Blue'. Then explain what happens to that measure's result if the report already has a slicer filtering Product[Color] to 'Red' when 'Blue Revenue' is displayed.
questions.code: -- Model: Sales[SalesAmount], 'Product'[Color], related by a relationship
questions.modelAnswer: CALCULATE evaluates an expression inside a modified filter context: CALCULATE(<expression>, <filter1>, <filter2>, ...). Blue Revenue = CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]), 'Product'[Color] = "Blue") sums SalesAmount but only for rows where Product[Color] equals 'Blue'. When a filter argument targets a column that's already filtered elsewhere in the report (like a slicer set to 'Red'), CALCULATE's filter overwrites the existing one for that expression rather than combining with it -- so Blue Revenue still shows blue-only totals even with the Red slicer active, because CALCULATE's explicit filter on Color replaces whatever the slicer was doing to that same column.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write it as CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]), 'Product'[Color] = "Blue"). The part I'd specifically call out in an interview is the overwrite behavior: if a report already has a slicer set to Color = 'Red', my Blue Revenue measure doesn't get combined with that -- it overwrites it for this expression, because CALCULATE's filter argument always wins over an existing filter on the same column. So no matter what the user has selected in that slicer, Blue Revenue keeps showing blue-only totals, which is exactly the point: CALCULATE lets me force a measure to ignore what the user selected and substitute my own condition instead.
questions.example:
Blue Revenue = CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]), 'Product'[Color] = "Blue")
-- Even with a report-level slicer set to Color = "Red", this measure
-- still returns blue-only totals, because CALCULATE's filter argument
-- overwrites the existing filter on the same column for this expression.
commonMistakes: Writing SUMX or FILTER where a simple CALCULATE + Boolean filter argument would be clearer and sufficient
Assuming CALCULATE's filter combines (ANDs) with an existing slicer on the same column instead of overwriting it
Forgetting the expression argument (SUM(...)) is what's actually being calculated -- the rest are just filter conditions
Quoting the table name incorrectly when the table name contains a space (needs 'Product' with quotes if there's a space, e.g. 'Reseller Sales')
keyPoints: CALCULATE(<expression>, <filter1>, ...) evaluates an expression in a modified filter context
A filter argument on an already-filtered column overwrites that filter for this expression
This overwrite behavior is what makes CALCULATE able to ignore user selections deliberately
KEEPFILTERS exists specifically to change this default overwrite behavior when needed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct CALCULATE syntax for the measure
Correctly explains the overwrite behavior against the Red slicer
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: Inflated totals after a new relationship
questions.prompt: A Power BI report's total sales figure looks inflated after a new relationship was added between two tables, and that relationship's cardinality was automatically set to 'one to one.' What might be wrong, and how would incorrect cardinality cause this?
questions.modelAnswer: Power BI sets cardinality to one-to-one automatically when it notices a value never repeats on either side of the relationship at the time the relationship is created. If the underlying data later changes so that one side starts legitimately repeating values (for example, a second budget row gets added for the same project in a later refresh), that one-to-one relationship no longer reflects reality, and Power BI's query engine will treat each row match as unique when it isn't -- a many-side table with duplicated keys joined as if it were one-to-one can fan out matching rows and inflate a SUM measure, because the engine isn't aggregating correctly across what are actually multiple matching rows per key. The fix is to open Manage relationships, edit the relationship, and override the cardinality to 'many to one' (or 'one to many'), explicitly pointing the 'many' side at the table that actually repeats values, rather than trusting Power BI's automatic detection once the data's shape has changed.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move would be Manage relationships, to actually see what cardinality Power BI chose and why. One-to-one only gets picked automatically because, at the moment the relationship was created, Power BI genuinely didn't see any repeated values on either side -- but that's a snapshot of the data at one point in time, not a guarantee. If a later refresh adds a second row for the same key on one side -- say a second budget line for a project that used to have exactly one -- the relationship is now lying about the data's actual shape, and a SUM measure built on top of it can double-count or otherwise misbehave because the engine is still treating the join as strictly one-to-one. The fix is straightforward once I've diagnosed it: edit the relationship and explicitly set cardinality to many-to-one, with the 'many' side pointed at whichever table I know will eventually repeat values, rather than leaving it to Power BI's automatic guess.
commonMistakes: Trusting Power BI's automatically-detected cardinality permanently instead of re-checking it after the data's shape changes
Not realizing one-to-one is only ever a snapshot judgment based on the data present when the relationship was created
Looking everywhere except Manage relationships when a total looks wrong after a schema change
Not knowing which side of a mismatched relationship should be set to 'many'
keyPoints: Power BI auto-detects one-to-one only when no repeats exist on either side at creation time
If repeats appear later, a stale one-to-one relationship can cause incorrect aggregation
Check and, if needed, manually override cardinality in Manage relationships
Point the 'many' side at whichever table is known to eventually repeat values

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses stale/incorrect cardinality as the likely cause
Explains how that causes inflated aggregation
Proposes the correct fix (Manage relationships, override cardinality)

questions.title: Why star schema helps the query engine
questions.prompt: Why does Power BI's query engine work better with a star schema -- one fact table surrounded by directly-connected dimension tables -- than with tables chained together in a snowflake or a loop?
questions.modelAnswer: A star schema connects one fact table at the center to dimension tables around it, each one joined directly to the fact table by its own relationship -- so filters flow inward from every dimension to the fact table along a single, predictable path. When a report visual spans two dimensions (say, sales by region compared to sales by product), the query has to travel through the fact table to connect them, and in a star schema there's exactly one route to do that. In a model where tables chain together in a loop or a long sequence (a snowflake, or dimensions connected to each other instead of only to the fact table), a filter can have more than one possible path to reach the same table, and Power BI can't always determine which path is intended -- which produces ambiguous or unexpected filtering behavior. A star schema avoids that entirely because every dimension has exactly one, direct route to the fact table, giving the engine an unambiguous path for every question a report asks.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe it in terms of how a filter actually travels through the model. In a star schema, every dimension connects straight to the fact table and nowhere else, so when a report visual asks a cross-dimension question -- sales by region versus sales by product, say -- there's exactly one path for that filter to travel: dimension to fact table. If instead I chain dimensions to each other, or let relationships form a loop, a filter might have two different ways to reach the same table, and the engine genuinely can't always tell which one I meant, which shows up as reports that filter in ways I didn't expect. Star schema isn't a stylistic preference -- it's what gives the engine a single, unambiguous path for every question, which is exactly why this course keeps coming back to 'one fact table, dimensions directly around it' as the default shape to build toward.
commonMistakes: Treating star schema as a cosmetic/organizational preference rather than something that affects query correctness
Not recognizing that a snowflake or looped model can create ambiguous filter paths
Building hierarchies across multiple separate dimension tables instead of within one, losing the single-table drill-down benefit
Mixing fact and dimension columns in the same table instead of keeping each table clearly one type or the other
keyPoints: Star schema: one fact table, dimensions connected directly to it, one path per filter
A chained/looped model can create ambiguous filter paths the engine can't resolve
Hierarchies belong inside a single dimension table, not spread across several
Keep tables clearly fact or dimension, never mixed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the single-path filter-flow advantage
Correctly contrasts with ambiguous paths in a snowflake/loop
Clarity and use of a concrete example

questions.title: Creating a static RLS role
questions.prompt: Describe the steps to create a static row-level security (RLS) role in Power BI Desktop named 'West Sales' that restricts a report to only show rows where Region equals 'West.' Why can't you finish testing or assigning users to this role entirely inside Desktop?
questions.modelAnswer: In Desktop, go to the Modeling tab and select Manage Roles, then New. Name the role 'West Sales' (commas aren't allowed in role names). Under Select tables, pick the table holding the Region column -- for example DimSalesTerritory. Under Filter data, use the default drop-down editor (since this is a simple static filter, not one needing a DAX function like USERPRINCIPALNAME()) and set the filter to [Region] = "West". Save, then publish the semantic model. Every DAX filter expression returns TRUE or FALSE per row, and only rows evaluating TRUE stay visible, so anyone later assigned to this role sees only rows where Region equals 'West.' You cannot assign users to the role from inside Desktop at all -- that step, along with fully testing the role as a specific user would see it, only exists once the semantic model is published to the Power BI service.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through it exactly as Desktop presents it: Modeling tab, Manage Roles, New, name it West Sales, pick the table that actually has the Region column -- DimSalesTerritory in an AdventureWorksDW2014-style model -- and since this is a plain static filter, the default drop-down editor is enough; I'd set it to [Region] = "West" rather than switching to the DAX editor, which I'd only need for something dynamic like USERPRINCIPALNAME(). Save, publish, done -- as far as Desktop is concerned. The thing I'd flag clearly is that creating the role and assigning a person to it are two completely separate steps in two completely separate places: Desktop only lets me define the rule, and assigning an actual user to 'West Sales' only happens once the model is in the Power BI service, so I can't fully test what a specific user would see until it's published.
commonMistakes: Trying to assign a user to the role from inside Power BI Desktop, which isn't possible there at all
Switching to the DAX editor unnecessarily for a simple static filter that the default editor already handles
Using a comma in the role name, which isn't allowed
Forgetting to publish the semantic model before assuming the role is usable anywhere
keyPoints: Manage Roles (Modeling tab) -> New -> name the role -> pick the table -> set the filter
Default editor handles static filters; DAX editor is needed only for dynamic ones (USERPRINCIPALNAME, etc.)
Every filter expression returns TRUE/FALSE per row; only TRUE rows stay visible
User assignment happens only in the Power BI service, never in Desktop

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct step-by-step role creation in Desktop
Correct static filter expression
Correctly explains the Desktop/service split for assignment

questions.title: Fact tables vs. dimension tables
questions.prompt: What's the difference between a fact table and a dimension table in a dimensional model, and why are dimension tables typically described as 'wide but short' while fact tables are described as 'narrow but tall'?
questions.modelAnswer: A fact table stores measurements about a business process at a defined grain -- mostly foreign keys to dimensions plus numeric measures -- and can grow into the billions of rows as events accumulate, while staying relatively narrow in column count. A dimension table stores the descriptive context used to filter and group those facts, sorted into four kinds of columns: a surrogate key, a natural key, descriptive attributes (the text columns actually filtered/grouped by), and sometimes foreign keys to other dimensions. Dimension tables are deliberately denormalized -- a product dimension stores its category and subcategory names directly on the same row instead of normalizing them into separate tables -- which adds columns but costs little, because a dimension table typically has only a few thousand rows. That's exactly why dimensions end up 'wide but short' (many columns, few rows) while fact tables end up 'narrow but tall' (few columns, potentially huge row counts): the denormalization trade-off only works out favorably because a dimension's row count stays small.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe a fact table as the 'what happened and how much' table -- mostly keys and numbers, one row per event at whatever grain was chosen, and it's the table that can genuinely reach billions of rows over time. A dimension table is the 'who, what, where, when' context around that -- names, categories, regions -- and it's deliberately denormalized on purpose: instead of normalizing Category, Subcategory, and Product into three separate tables the way an OLTP system would, a warehouse's DimProduct just stores all three as columns on the same row. That sounds wasteful until you look at the actual row counts: a product dimension might have a few thousand rows, so storing 'Bikes' redundantly on every one of them costs almost nothing, and in exchange I get to filter or group by category without an extra join. That's the whole reason dimensions end up wide but short while facts end up narrow but tall -- the trade-off only pays off because dimension row counts stay small.
commonMistakes: Normalizing a dimension table the way you would an OLTP system, losing the single-table hierarchy/no-extra-join benefit
Thinking denormalization in a dimension table is always a bad practice rather than a deliberate, cheap trade-off
Confusing which table type holds the measures (fact) versus the descriptive attributes (dimension)
Not recognizing that the 'wide but short vs. narrow but tall' distinction is exactly why the denormalization trade-off works
keyPoints: Fact table: mostly keys + measures, narrow, potentially huge row count
Dimension table: surrogate key, natural key, descriptive attributes, sometimes FKs to other dimensions
Dimension tables are deliberately denormalized to avoid extra joins
Dimensions are wide but short; facts are narrow but tall -- because dimension row counts stay small

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes fact vs. dimension table purpose
Correctly explains deliberate denormalization in dimensions
Explains the wide-but-short / narrow-but-tall framing

questions.title: SCD Type 1 vs. Type 2
questions.prompt: What's the difference between a Slowly Changing Dimension Type 1 and Type 2, and what real reporting problem does Type 2 solve that Type 1 can't?
questions.modelAnswer: SCD Type 1 overwrites the existing dimension row in place when an attribute changes -- no new row is inserted, the surrogate key doesn't change, and the old value leaves no trace. It's the simplest pattern and Microsoft's own guidance is that it should be the default for most changing attributes, especially corrections (a misspelled name) or attributes where history genuinely doesn't matter for analysis. Its real cost is that every historical fact joined to that dimension member now reports under the new value, even for events that happened before the change -- for example, reassigning a salesperson's region with a Type 1 update makes a 'historical sales by region' report show all of their past sales under the new region, as if they'd always been there. SCD Type 2 solves exactly that problem: instead of overwriting, it closes the old row (setting an ExpirationDate and flipping IsCurrentFlag to false) and inserts a brand-new row with a new surrogate key, the same natural key, the new attribute value, and IsCurrentFlag set to true. Because the old row is preserved untouched, historical facts loaded before the change still point at the old surrogate key and correctly reflect what was true at the time, while new facts point at the new version.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe Type 1 as the 'just fix it' pattern -- one UPDATE statement, the old value is gone, done -- and it's genuinely the right default for most attributes, since most changes (a corrected phone number, a fixed typo) aren't business events worth preserving history for. Type 2 is what I'd reach for specifically when history matters for reporting, and the mechanics are an UPDATE and an INSERT working together as one transaction: the old row gets its EndDate set and IsCurrent flipped to false, and a brand-new row is inserted with a new surrogate key, the same natural key, the new attribute, and IsCurrent set to true. The concrete problem this solves is a real one Microsoft's own documentation calls out: if a salesperson moves from one region to another and I used Type 1, every sale they ever made -- even the ones from before the move -- would retroactively show up under the new region in a historical rollup. Type 2 keeps the old surrogate key intact for those old facts, so the history stays accurate, at the cost of now having two (or more) rows to account for when analyzing that one salesperson.
commonMistakes: Using Type 1 by default for attributes where historical reporting accuracy actually matters
Forgetting Type 2 requires a surrogate key, since the natural key now repeats across versions
Omitting the IsCurrentFlag/ExpirationDate columns, making it impossible to easily query only the current version
Not treating the UPDATE + INSERT pair as one atomic transaction representing a single business event
keyPoints: Type 1 overwrites in place; no history, simplest default for most attributes
Type 1's cost: historical facts retroactively reflect the new value
Type 2 inserts a new versioned row and closes the old one; requires a surrogate key
Type 2's tracking columns: EffectiveDate/ExpirationDate/IsCurrentFlag

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes Type 1 mechanics and its retroactive-rollup risk
Correctly describes Type 2 mechanics (update + insert, surrogate key)
Clearly states what business problem Type 2 solves

questions.title: Choosing the grain for a sales fact table
questions.prompt: You're designing a fact table for online sales that needs to answer both 'how many orders did we take' and 'which specific products were on each order.' Write a precise, one-sentence grain statement for this fact table, and explain why a coarser grain statement (one row per order) would fail to answer the second question.
questions.modelAnswer: The grain statement should be: 'one row per order line.' Grain is a one-sentence statement of exactly what a single fact table row represents, and it has to be declared before any column is chosen, because every dimension key and measure a fact table can legitimately hold is determined by its grain. A 'one row per order' grain can answer 'how many orders did we take,' but it cannot answer which products were on any order, because a product key isn't meaningful at the order level -- an order can contain multiple products, so there's no single ProductKey to attach to an order-level row. At the order-line grain, a ProductKey belongs naturally, because every line genuinely has exactly one product. This is also why Kimball's standard advice is to build at the atomic (finest-detail) grain first: atomic data can answer questions you haven't thought to ask yet, while a coarser, summarized grain can only answer questions that fit the level it was already rolled up to.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write the grain as 'one row per order line' and explain why that single sentence has to come before any column gets named. If I'd instead declared the grain as 'one row per order,' I could still answer 'how many orders did we take in March' just fine, but the moment someone asks 'which products were on those orders,' I'm stuck -- an order can have several products on it, so there's no single, unambiguous ProductKey to put on an order-level row. At the order-line grain, every row genuinely has exactly one product, so ProductKey fits naturally without forcing anything. I'd also flag the broader principle here: Kimball's advice is almost always to go atomic first, because atomic-grain data can still answer a question nobody's thought to ask yet, while a table that was already summarized up to order-level can only ever answer the questions that fit that level -- asking for finer detail later means reprocessing from the source all over again.
questions.example:
GRAIN: one row per order line
-- ProductKey belongs on this row: every line has exactly one product.
-- A coarser "one row per order" grain cannot carry ProductKey at all,
-- since one order can contain several different products.
commonMistakes: Writing a grain statement with an 'and' or an 'or' in it, which signals two different grains mixed into one table
Choosing a summarized grain first for performance reasons instead of building the atomic grain and adding aggregates later
Trying to force an order-level grain to also carry product-level detail, resulting in repeated or null columns
Not declaring the grain in plain English before naming any columns
keyPoints: Grain is a one-sentence statement of what one row represents, declared before any column
Order-line grain supports a ProductKey; order grain does not
Kimball's standard advice: build atomic grain first, summarize later if needed
A grain statement containing 'and'/'or' is a warning sign of mixed grain

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Writes a correct, precise grain statement
Correctly explains why the coarser grain fails the second question
Mentions the atomic-grain-first principle

questions.title: When a Type 1 update breaks historical reporting
questions.prompt: After a salesperson is reassigned from the East region to the West region, your Type 1 dimension update runs exactly as designed -- and now a 'historical sales by region' report shows all of that salesperson's past sales under West, even sales made while they were still assigned to East. Is this a bug? What would you do differently if the business actually needs accurate historical reporting here?
questions.modelAnswer: This isn't a bug -- it's Type 1 working exactly as designed. Type 1 overwrites the existing dimension row in place with no history preserved, so every historical fact joined to that dimension member now reports using the new value, as if it had always been true, regardless of when the fact actually occurred. The real issue is that Type 1 was the wrong pattern to apply to this attribute given the business's reporting needs. The fix is to reclassify the SalesRegionKey attribute on this dimension as Type 2 instead: when the salesperson's region changes, close the existing row (set its ExpirationDate and flip IsCurrentFlag to false) and insert a new row with a new surrogate key, the same natural key, the new region, and IsCurrentFlag true. Because the old row stays intact under its original surrogate key, historical facts that were loaded while the salesperson was still assigned to East continue to point at that old row and correctly report under East, while new facts point at the new West version.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd be clear with the business that this isn't a defect -- it's exactly what Type 1 is supposed to do, which is overwrite with no memory of the old value. The mistake was choosing Type 1 for an attribute that this specific report actually needs history for. If accurate historical-by-region reporting matters, I'd migrate SalesRegionKey on this dimension to a Type 2 pattern: the next time the region changes, instead of one UPDATE, it becomes an UPDATE that closes the old row (ExpirationDate, IsCurrentFlag = false) plus an INSERT that opens a new row with a new surrogate key and the new region, run together as one transaction. Going forward, facts loaded before the change keep pointing at the old surrogate key and still show East correctly, while facts loaded after point at the new one and show West -- which is the entire reason Type 2 exists, and exactly the trade-off Type 1 couldn't give me.
commonMistakes: Treating this as a software bug rather than recognizing it's Type 1 behaving exactly as designed
Not identifying that the fix is a change to the SCD pattern for this attribute, not a code fix
Forgetting a Type 2 migration also requires adding a surrogate key if one wasn't already in place

Assuming existing historical facts would automatically re-point to a correct historical value after switching to Type 2 -- data already loaded under the overwritten Type 1 row can't retroactively recover lost history
keyPoints: This is expected Type 1 behavior, not a bug -- Type 1 keeps no history by design
The real problem is choosing Type 1 for an attribute that needed historical accuracy
Fix: migrate the attribute to Type 2 (close old row, insert new versioned row)
Type 2 requires a surrogate key so old and new versions are independently addressable

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies this as expected Type 1 behavior, not a bug
Correctly proposes migrating the attribute to Type 2
Notes the limitation that already-lost history can't be recovered retroactively

questions.title: Walk through a BI project end to end
questions.prompt: Walk me through a BI project you've built end to end -- from raw source data to a report a business user would actually look at. What tool did each stage use, and why that tool for that stage?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer names a concrete pipeline rather than describing tools in the abstract: raw source tables in SQL Server, an SSIS package that moves and transforms data from a staging table into a warehouse fact table and its dimensions, an SSRS paginated report built against that warehouse for fixed, printable, grouped reporting, and a Power BI report connecting to the same warehouse independently for interactive, trend-based visuals. The answer should explain why each tool was chosen for its stage: SSIS for scheduled, server-side ETL that needs to run unattended and handle error cases; a warehouse with a deliberately chosen grain and real fact/dimension design (for example, an accumulating snapshot fact table like one tracking a work order through its lifecycle) so the same clean data serves multiple downstream consumers; SSRS for a fixed, operational, paginated report a business user prints or exports; Power BI for interactive exploration, filtering, and dashboard-style visuals that a paginated report isn't suited for. SSRS and Power BI should be described as two independent consumers of one shared warehouse, not as feeding each other.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through my capstone project the way I actually built it, naming real objects instead of speaking in generalities. Raw data lived in AdventureWorks2012's Production tables. I built an SSIS package that staged it and loaded it into a warehouse fact table I modeled as an accumulating snapshot, because the thing it tracked -- a work order -- gets revisited and updated as it moves through production, not inserted once and left alone. From there, two completely separate tools read the same warehouse: an SSRS paginated report gave operations a fixed, grouped-by-product report they could export or print, and a Power BI report connected independently and built the trend and comparison visuals a paginated report just isn't designed for -- things like a scrap-rate trend over time. I'd specifically call out that neither tool fed the other; they're two independent consumers of one shared, well-modeled warehouse, which is really the entire point of building the warehouse in the first place rather than letting each report reinvent its own data prep.
commonMistakes: Describing tools in the abstract ('I know SSIS, SSRS, and Power BI') instead of naming a specific, real pipeline
Not explaining why each tool fits its stage, just listing them in sequence
Implying SSRS and Power BI feed into each other, rather than both reading the same underlying warehouse independently
Skipping the warehouse/data-modeling stage entirely and jumping straight from source data to reports
keyPoints: Name real, specific objects (tables, packages, reports), not generic tool names
Explain why each tool fits its stage, not just that it was used
The warehouse is the shared foundation both SSRS and Power BI read independently
Mention the grain/fact-table design decision behind the warehouse if possible

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a concrete, specific pipeline rather than generic tool names
Explains why each tool/stage was chosen
Clearly communicates the end-to-end flow

questions.title: Tell me about a time you debugged something unexpected
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you had to debug something that wasn't behaving the way you expected -- a package, a report, or a query that returned the wrong numbers. How did you track down the cause?
questions.modelAnswer: This is a behavioral question testing how a candidate works under pressure and communicates about a technical problem, not a request for a specific technical fact. A strong answer uses the STAR structure: Situation (brief context -- what project, what was happening), Task (what the candidate was specifically responsible for), Action (the actual debugging steps taken, which is the bulk of the answer), and Result (the concrete outcome, stated directly rather than left implied -- ideally with a number or a specific fixed state). The most commonly skipped beat is Result; candidates often describe the problem and the fix in detail, then stop without stating what actually happened afterward. The best source material for a career-changer is a real moment from their own project work -- a package that failed silently, a fact table that wouldn't balance against the source until a join was traced, or a report returning numbers that didn't match expectations until a specific cause was isolated.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell this as one specific, real story rather than a general description of how I debug things. Situation: while building my capstone's SSIS package, the warehouse load finished without any error, but the fact table's row count didn't match what I expected from the source. Task: I needed to find where rows were being silently dropped. Action: I isolated each transformation one at a time with data viewers until I found a Lookup transformation that was rejecting non-matching rows without any visible error, because its error output wasn't connected to anything -- it was just quietly discarding them. I wired the error output into a flat-file destination so the rejected rows became visible instead of invisible, and traced those back to a handful of rows with a ScrapReasonID that didn't yet exist in the dimension. Result: once I fixed the dimension load order so the dimension populated before the fact table referenced it, the row counts matched exactly, and I had a permanent, visible log of any future rejected rows instead of a silent gap. I'd keep this under about two minutes and make sure I actually land that last sentence instead of trailing off.
commonMistakes: Skipping the Result beat and trailing off after describing the fix, instead of stating the concrete outcome
Describing debugging skills in general terms instead of telling one specific, real story
Spending too long on Situation detail and running past two minutes before reaching the actual Action
Inventing a generic workplace story instead of using a real moment from actual project work
keyPoints: Use the STAR structure: Situation, Task, Action, Result
Result is the most commonly skipped beat -- state the concrete outcome explicitly
Use a specific, real debugging moment, not a general description of debugging skill
Keep the whole answer to roughly two minutes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Uses a clear STAR structure
Tells a specific, real, technically grounded story
States a concrete, explicit Result

questions.title: Explaining star schema to a non-technical stakeholder
questions.prompt: How would you explain what a 'star schema' is to a non-technical stakeholder who just asked why the BI team needs to 'restructure the data' before they can build a dashboard?
questions.modelAnswer: This question tests whether a candidate can translate a real technical concept into plain language a non-technical stakeholder can act on, without dumbing it down to the point of being inaccurate. A strong answer avoids jargon like 'cardinality' or 'denormalization' and instead uses a concrete analogy: organizing the data the way a reporting tool can quickly use it, with one central table of 'what happened' (sales, orders) surrounded by a small number of reference tables describing 'who, what, where, when' (customers, products, dates) -- so every question the dashboard asks has one clear, fast path to the answer instead of the tool getting confused about which table relates to which. The answer should connect this directly to the stakeholder's actual concern: this restructuring is what makes the dashboard fast and reliable, and skipping it is what causes dashboards to be slow or to show inconsistent numbers later.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd skip the term 'star schema' entirely in the actual explanation and focus on what it does for them. I'd say something like: right now the data is organized the way it's easiest to enter and update, which is great for the system that runs day-to-day operations, but it's not organized the way a reporting tool can quickly answer questions. What we're doing is putting one central table of 'what happened' -- your sales, your orders -- in the middle, and a small number of simple reference tables around it for things like which customer, which product, and which date, each connected directly to that center table. That way, when you ask the dashboard 'show me sales by region and by product,' there's exactly one clear path for it to follow, instead of the tool getting confused trying to guess which table relates to which. I'd close with the stakes in their terms: skip this step, and the dashboard you get is either going to be slow, or it's going to show numbers that don't quite add up the way you expect -- this restructuring is what prevents both of those.
commonMistakes: Using technical jargon (cardinality, denormalization, dimensional modeling) without translating it
Explaining the concept accurately but never connecting it back to the stakeholder's actual concern (why this matters for their dashboard)
Being so simplified the explanation becomes inaccurate rather than just jargon-free
Making the stakeholder feel talked down to instead of genuinely informed
keyPoints: Avoid technical jargon; use a plain-language analogy instead
Center table = 'what happened'; surrounding tables = descriptive context
Connect the explanation directly to the stakeholder's actual concern (speed, reliability)
Stay accurate while staying simple -- don't oversimplify into something wrong

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains the concept accurately without technical jargon
Uses a clear, relatable analogy
Connects the explanation to the stakeholder's actual concern
